claims.claim: Economics is the study of how people and societies choose to employ scarce productive resources that have alternative uses; the modern working definition is attributed to Paul Samuelson, with Lionel Robbins (1932) as an earlier source.
Scarcity means human wants for goods, services, and resources exceed what is available, and every society at every level must make choices about how to use its resources.

Economics has two main subareas: macroeconomics is the study of the economy as a whole (aggregates such as national output and total employment), while microeconomics focuses on individual parts such as households and firms.
Demand is the quantity of a good or service people are willing to buy at various prices, and the quantity demanded falls as the price rises.
Supply is the quantity of a good or service businesses will make available at various prices, and the quantity supplied rises as the price rises.
The market price settles at the equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; a surplus pushes prices down and a shortage pulls prices up.
Competition in a market leads to better and more diverse products and keeps prices stable; when profits are high, new sellers enter, and the resulting competition tends to lower prices.
The level of economic activity is constantly changing; these upward and downward changes are called business cycles, and they vary in length, severity, and how much the economy is affected.

Expansions are periods between a trough and a peak, and recessions are periods between a peak and a trough; a recession is a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting more than a few months.
Business-cycle turning points are dated retrospectively: the NBER waits until sufficient data are available, so recession timing is confirmed only after the fact and cannot be forecast reliably.

The state of the economy affects business decisions about what products to produce, how to price them, how many people to employ, and how much to pay them; businesses must monitor and react to the phases of the business cycle.

The supply-and-demand model is a simplification that assumes conditions such as perfect competition, which rarely hold fully in real markets, so it describes tendencies rather than precise real-world predictions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What exactly counts as a recession
positions: Popular shorthand: two consecutive quarters of falling real GDP.

NBER's official U.S. dating approach: a significant decline in economic activity spread across the economy and lasting more than a few months, judged across many monthly and quarterly indicators, not GDP alone.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NBER-style definition (significant, economy-wide, lasting decline) and emphasizes that turning points are dated retrospectively; it avoids the two-quarter shorthand and makes no forecasts.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How well the supply-and-demand model describes real markets
positions: Textbook treatment: price settles where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, with surpluses and shortages driving adjustment.

CFI and OpenStax both note the framework assumes conditions, such as many similar sellers and informed buyers (perfect competition), that rarely hold fully; real markets have few sellers, differentiated products, and imperfect information.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents supply and demand as the core price-setting framework but pairs it with the honest-framing caveat that models describe pressures, not exact predictions.

positions: Some economists emphasize fluctuations in aggregate demand (Keynesian explanations).
Others emphasize technology and productivity shocks (real business cycle explanations).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names expansions and recessions as recurring patterns and deliberately does not endorse any theory of causation, keeping to the general-education scope.

sourceRecords.title: Business Cycle
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: a business cycle is a cycle of fluctuations in economic activity around its long-term growth rate, explaining expansion and contraction over time; in the expansion stage employment, income, output, wages, and profits rise; the recession stage follows the peak, with demand declining and unemployment rising; cycles are completed through peak, recession, trough, and recovery. Used for the named phases of the business cycle. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Economics - Definition, Types & Key Concepts Explained
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the modern working definition of economics, attributed to 20th-century economist Paul Samuelson, is the study of how people and society choose, with or without the use of money, to employ scarce productive resources which could have alternative uses to produce various commodities over time and distribute them for consumption; Lionel Robbins (1932) defined economics as the science studying human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses. Used for the attributed working definition of economics. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Supply and Demand
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B reference. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the laws of supply and demand are microeconomic concepts stating that in efficient markets the quantity supplied and the quantity demanded of a good are equal, and the price is determined at the point where they meet; as price increases, supply increases (seller perspective) and demand decreases (buyer perspective); the framework assumes conditions such as perfect competition that rarely hold in real life. Used for the supply-demand core and the honest-framing caveat. Facts synthesized; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, 1.4 Macroeconomics: The Big Picture
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21. Supports: the level of economic activity is constantly changing, and these upward and downward changes are called business cycles; cycles vary in length, in how high or low the economy moves, and in how much the economy is affected; an increase in business activity brings rising output, income, employment, and prices until activity peaks and then declines; businesses must monitor and react to cycle phases - during growth, hiring and scarce supplies get harder, and during a recession firms find more capacity than demand requires.
